objectives: I can describe how a browser requests a page from a web server and the roles of HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
I can write and interpret HTML using the tags and attributes OCR names, correctly nested.
I can style a page with CSS element, class and id selectors placed inline, internally or in an external stylesheet.
I can write simple JavaScript including form validation, and compare client-side with server-side processing.

retrieval.q: 1.3.3: Give two differences between a LAN and a WAN.
retrieval.a: A LAN covers a small geographical area (one site) and is usually owned/maintained by one organisation; a WAN covers a large geographical area and uses third-party communication infrastructure (e.g. leased lines). The internet is the largest WAN.

retrieval.q: 1.3.3: Name the four layers of the TCP/IP stack in order, from the layer nearest the user downwards.
retrieval.a: Application, Transport, Network (Internet), Link (Data link). Data passes down the stack on sending, each layer adding a header, and back up on receipt.

retrieval.q: 1.3.3: What does DNS do when you type www.ocr.org.uk into a browser?
retrieval.a: The Domain Name System translates the human-readable domain name into the IP address of the server, querying resolver/root/TLD/authoritative servers as needed and caching the result.

retrieval.q: 1.3.3: State two differences between packet switching and circuit switching.
retrieval.a: Packet switching splits data into packets that are routed independently and may take different routes, then reassembled; circuit switching sets up one dedicated path for the whole communication, reserving bandwidth even when idle. The internet uses packet switching.

retrieval.q: 1.3.3: In a client-server network, what is the role of the server, and what is the main structural difference in peer-to-peer?
retrieval.a: The server provides resources/services to clients that request them, giving central control and backup; in peer-to-peer all devices have equal status and each can act as both client and server.

keywords.def: HyperText Markup Language: defines the structure and content of a web page using tags such as h1, p, img and a.
Cascading Style Sheets: defines presentation and style such as colour, font, borders and layout, kept separate from structure.
A scripting language giving client-side interactivity and behaviour: responding to events, validating forms and updating content dynamically.
A tag marks up content (e.g. img); an attribute inside the opening tag gives extra detail (e.g. src, alt, href, class, id).
The part of a CSS rule that says which elements to style: a bare tag name, a .class or an #id.
A reusable label attached with class="name" in HTML and targeted with .name in CSS; many elements may share one class.
A unique label attached with id="name" and targeted with #name in CSS; each id must appear only once per page.
Code that runs in the user's browser: fast and reduces server load, but can be viewed and bypassed, so it is not secure.
Code that runs on the web server: secure, hidden and able to use server databases, but slower and adds server load.

content.heading: How the web works: request and response
points: The browser (client) sends an HTTP or HTTPS request for a page to a web server.
The server responds with HTML; the browser renders it, fetching any linked CSS, JavaScript and images.
HTML defines structure and content; CSS defines presentation and style; JavaScript defines behaviour and interactivity.
Keeping the three separate makes sites maintainable: restyle a whole site without touching structure or behaviour.
content.note: Search engines, indexing and PageRank use these same pages — that is next lesson (part 2).

content.heading: HTML page structure and nesting
points: A page nests inside html: the head holds information about the page, the body holds visible content.
title sits inside head and names the browser tab; it does not appear in the page itself.
Most tags come in opening/closing pairs and must nest correctly: always close the inner tag first.

content.heading: Content tags: headings, paragraphs, images, links, div
points: h1 to h6 are headings from largest to smallest; p marks a paragraph of text.
img has no closing tag: src names the image file, alt gives text shown if it cannot load.
a makes a hyperlink: href gives the destination; the text between the tags is what users click.
div groups a block of elements so it can be styled or scripted as one unit.

content.heading: Lists, forms, script and link
points: ol creates a numbered list and ul a bulleted list; every item inside is an li.
form collects user input; input creates a control, and its type attribute sets the kind (text, submit).
script embeds JavaScript or loads it from a file; link in the head attaches an external stylesheet.

content.heading: CSS: purpose and three places to put it
points: Inline: a style attribute on one tag — quick, but mixes style back into the structure.
Internal: rules inside a style tag in the head — applies to that one page only.
External: a separate .css file attached with link — one file styles every page (best practice).
Common properties: color, background-color, font-family, border, width, height, text-align.
code: Inline style on one tag
content.note: One edit to an external stylesheet restyles the whole site — the advantage examiners reward.

content.heading: CSS selectors: elements, classes and identifiers
points: An element selector (h1) styles every matching tag on the page.
A class selector (.warning) styles every element carrying class="warning" — reusable on many elements.
An id selector (#menu) styles the single element with id="menu" — each id is unique per page.
In the HTML, the class= and id= attributes are what connect elements to the rules.
code: #menu { width: 200px; height: 400px; background-color: grey; border: 1px solid black; }

content.heading: JavaScript basics: variables, functions, events
points: Variables (var or let) store values; functions package reusable code, much like pseudocode.
Events such as onclick run a function when the user acts on the page.
document.getElementById("x") fetches an element; .value reads an input box; .innerHTML changes displayed content.
Styles can be changed too, e.g. element.style.color = "red".

content.heading: JavaScript form validation
points: Validation checks input is present and sensible before the form is submitted to the server.
Read the box with getElementById and .value, test it with if, and alert the user on failure.
Returning false stops the submission; returning true lets the form send.
content.note: Client-side validation improves user experience but can be viewed and bypassed — never rely on it alone.

content.heading: Client-side processing
points: Runs in the user's browser: form validation, instant feedback, animation, updating content without reloading.
Advantages: fast and immediate (no round trip to the server); reduces server load and bandwidth.
Disadvantages: the code can be viewed, modified or disabled by the user, so it is insecure.
It also depends on the user's browser and device behaving as expected.

content.heading: Server-side processing: when it must be used
points: Runs on the web server (e.g. PHP with SQL): login checks, payments, searching a product database.
Must be used when logic or data has to stay secure, or when the data lives in a server database.
Client-side: fast, low server load, insecure. Server-side: secure, hidden, database access, but slower and loads the server.
Best practice: validate client-side for speed and repeat the checks server-side for security.

worked_examples.title: Building a small page: which selector styles what?
steps:
The HTML: Clubs

Code Club

Meets Tuesday lunchtime.

Open to all years.

Bring a laptop.
The external stylesheet styles.css: h1 { color: navy; text-align: center; }  .highlight { background-color: yellow; }  #pageTitle { border: 2px solid black; }
Rule 1 is an element selector: it styles every h1 — here just one — navy and centred.
Rule 2 is a class selector: it highlights the first and third paragraphs, because both carry class="highlight". A class is reusable on many elements.
Rule 3 is an id selector: it puts a border on the single element with id="pageTitle" — the h1. An id must be unique on the page.
So the h1 receives two rules (element and id) and the middle paragraph receives none — it has no class or id and no p rule exists.
Because the stylesheet is external, adding the same link tag to another page restyles it identically with no extra CSS.

worked_examples.title: Tracing a JavaScript validation function
steps: The function: function checkForm() { var name = document.getElementById("name").value; var age = Number(document.getElementById("age").value); if (name == "") { alert("Please enter your name"); return false; } if (age < 11 || age > 18) { alert("Age must be 11 to 18"); return false; } return true; }
It reads the two input boxes by id, converts age to a number, then tests each rule in turn.
Trace 1 — name is empty, age is 14: the first if is true, so the alert Please enter your name appears and the function returns false. The age test is never reached; the form does not submit.

Trace 2 — name is Sam, age is 21: name is not empty, so the first if is skipped. In the second if, 21 < 11 is false but 21 > 18 is true, so with OR the condition is true: alert Age must be 11 to 18, return false.
Trace 3 — name is Ada, age is 16: both ifs are false (16 is within 11 to 18), so the function returns true and the form submits.
Key idea: return false blocks submission, and the || means either failing bound rejects the age.

worked_examples.title: Client-side or server-side? A login flow
steps: A login page asks for a username and password. Decide where each processing step belongs.
Checking the boxes are not empty before sending: client-side. It is not security-critical, gives instant feedback, and saves a pointless round trip, reducing server load.
Checking the password against the stored password hash: server-side, always. The stored hashes and comparison logic must stay hidden on the server.
Why it cannot be client-side: any code sent to the browser can be viewed, modified or bypassed, so a client-side check would expose the hash and could simply be skipped.
Recording the successful login in the accounts database: server-side, because the database lives on the server.

Conclusion: client-side for speed and user experience, server-side for anything secret, security-critical or database-driven — and security checks are repeated server-side even if the client also checks.

activities.title: Client-side vs server-side continuum
instructions: Tape a line across the room: client-side at one end, server-side at the other; standing in the middle means needs both.

Think for 30 seconds, pair for 30, then stand on the line for each scenario: highlighting a menu button on hover; checking a typed password against the stored hash; warning that the email field is empty; searching the product database for trainers; validating a card payment; form validation on a banking site.
Interview outliers each round: what happens to the server if we move this to the client, and what happens to security?

Board the trade-off summary: speed, responsiveness and reduced server load versus security and access to the database. The banking form is the exam-grade answer: both — client-side for fast feedback, repeated server-side because browser code can be bypassed.

practice.q: State the purpose of each of HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a web page. [3]
practice.a: HTML defines the structure and content of the page (1); CSS defines the presentation/style such as colours, fonts and layout (1); JavaScript adds interactivity/behaviour such as responding to events and validating forms (1).

practice.q: Write the HTML to display an image stored as logo.png, with the alternative text School logo. [2]
practice.a: — one mark for the img tag with correct src attribute, one for the alt attribute.

practice.q: A stylesheet contains the rule .alert { color: red; }. Describe how a developer applies this rule to a paragraph, and explain one difference between a class and an id. [3]
practice.a:
Add the attribute to the tag:

(1). A class can be reused on many elements on the page (1), whereas an id must be unique — used on only one element — and is targeted with # rather than . (1).

practice.q: Write a CSS rule that gives the element with the identifier menu a width of 200 pixels and a grey background. [3]
practice.a: #menu { width: 200px; background-color: grey; } — one mark for the #menu selector, one for width: 200px;, one for background-color: grey;.

practice.q: Write a JavaScript function named checkEmail that displays an alert saying Please enter your email if the text box with the id email is empty. [4]
practice.a: function checkEmail() { var email = document.getElementById("email").value; if (email == "") { alert("Please enter your email"); } } — marks for the function declaration, using document.getElementById("email").value, the comparison with the empty string, and the alert inside the if.

practice.q: Explain two advantages of validating a form using client-side JavaScript rather than on the server. [4]
practice.a: The user gets an immediate response (1) because no round trip to the server is needed (1); and server load/bandwidth is reduced (1) because invalid submissions are stopped before they are ever sent (1).

practice.q: A website checks a user's password when they log in. Explain why this check must be carried out server-side. [3]
practice.a: Client-side code can be viewed, modified or bypassed by the user (1), so a browser check cannot be trusted for security (1); the stored password data/hashes and the comparison logic must stay hidden on the server, which also holds the accounts database (1).

practice.q: Describe the difference between an internal and an external stylesheet, and give one advantage of using an external stylesheet. [3]
practice.a: An internal stylesheet is written in a style tag in the head and applies to that page only (1); an external stylesheet is a separate .css file attached with a link tag (1). Advantage: one file can style every page of the site, so a single change updates the whole site consistently (1).

misconceptions: Students often write colour in CSS because of UK spelling, but the property names are color and background-color — colour is simply ignored by the browser.
Students often treat class and id as interchangeable, but an id must be unique to one element per page (#name), while a class is designed to be reused on many elements (.name).
Students often think client-side validation makes a form secure, but browser code can be viewed, altered or bypassed, so every security-critical check must be repeated server-side.
Students often mix up the attributes: img uses src for the file, while a uses href for the destination — swapping them is a classic exam-code error.
Students often think JavaScript is a cut-down version of Java, but they are unrelated languages; JavaScript is the scripting language browsers run client-side.
exam_link: Command words: state and write for tags, attributes and CSS rules (1 mark per correct piece of syntax); describe and explain for validation and processing; compare for client-side versus server-side.
Typical tariffs: 2-3 marks to write an HTML tag or CSS rule; 3-4 marks for short JavaScript; 4-6 marks to explain or compare client-side and server-side processing in context.
Example stem: A form on a shopping website is validated using JavaScript in the browser. Explain why the data entered must also be validated on the web server. [3]
Code answers are marked on exact syntax: src versus href, . versus # selectors, matching closing tags and correct nesting all carry marks — sloppy syntax loses them.
task: Write, on paper, the complete HTML for a page titled Revision Hub containing: a main heading with the id title, two paragraphs sharing the class note, an image study.png with suitable alternative text, and a link to quiz.html with the text Start quiz. Then write an external stylesheet with three rules: an element selector centring all h1 text, a class selector giving .note a grey background, and an id selector giving #title a navy colour and a border. Annotate each rule with exactly which element(s) it styles and why.
challenge: Extend your page with a form containing a text input with the id score and a submit button, then write a JavaScript function that rejects the submission with an alert if the score is empty or not between 0 and 100. Trace your function for the inputs 150 and 72, then write two sentences explaining why a quiz website could not trust this check alone and what it must do instead.

exit_ticket.q: Which technology provides structure, which provides style, and which provides behaviour?
exit_ticket.a: HTML provides structure and content, CSS provides style/presentation, JavaScript provides behaviour/interactivity.

exit_ticket.q: In CSS, what is the difference between the selectors .menu and #menu?
exit_ticket.a: .menu targets every element with class="menu" (reusable on many elements); #menu targets the single element with id="menu" (an id is unique per page).

exit_ticket.q: Give one reason a login check must run server-side even if the form is also checked in the browser.
exit_ticket.a: Client-side code can be viewed and bypassed, so it is not secure; the stored password data and comparison must stay hidden on the server.
